method: Rebuild from primary text. Cal. Lab. Code §512 was fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (via the chapter text view, which shows the operative version) and §226.7 the same way — §226.7 has two enacted versions on file and both were read, the current one and the one Stats. 2020, Ch. 343, Sec. 3 makes operative January 1, 2027. IWC Order No. 4-2001 §11 was fetched from the Department of Industrial Relations, which is the body that publishes the wage orders. The clause body was then written from what those texts say and checked against the construing case law on CourtListener. Assertions below describe the REBUILT body; the previous body's errors are under priorDefects.
queries: Cal. Lab. Code §512 and §226.7 full text (leginfo)
Brinker meal period relieve of all duty need not ensure
"regular rate of compensation" "226.7" meal rest premium nondiscretionary
Donohue AMN Services rounding meal periods rebuttable presumption

assertions.text: the meal period duty attaches to a work period of more than five hours, and a second to more than ten
assertions.note: §512(a), verbatim: 'An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes ... shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes.' Wage Order 4 §11(A) is to the same effect for the first period.

assertions.text: the first period may be waived by mutual consent where the total work period is no more than six hours, and the second where the total is no more than twelve and the first was not waived
assertions.note: §512(a). Wage Order 4 §11(A) puts the first waiver as 'when a work period of not more than six (6) hours will complete the day's work'. The previous body did not mention waiver at all, which for a small employer running short shifts is the provision most likely to apply.

assertions.text: the employer must relieve the employee of all duty and relinquish control, but need not ensure that no work is done
assertions.note: Brinker, verbatim: 'an employer must relieve the employee of all duty for the designated period, but need not ensure that the employee does no work.' This is the holding the previous body inverted. It is why a break that was provided and worked through owes no premium.

assertions.text: an on-duty meal period is counted as time worked and is permitted only where the nature of the work prevents relief from all duty and there is a written, revocable agreement
assertions.note: Wage Order 4 §11(A), verbatim: 'Unless the employee is relieved of all duty during a 30 minute meal period, the meal period shall be considered an on-duty meal period and counted as time worked. An on-duty meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty and when by written agreement between the parties an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to. The written agreement shall state that the employee may, in writing, revoke the agreement at any time.' Absent from the previous body.

assertions.text: the premium is one additional hour of pay for each workday a compliant period is not provided
assertions.note: §226.7(c) and Wage Order 4 §11(B). Note the unit: per workday, not per missed period. The previous body's 'a missed, late, or interrupted meal period entitles the employee to one additional hour of pay' tied the premium to the break rather than to the employer's failure to provide, and stated no unit.

assertions.text: 'regular rate of compensation' in §226.7(c) means the same as 'regular rate of pay' for overtime and includes non-discretionary payments
assertions.note: Ferra v. Loews Hollywood Hotel, holding quoted below. The previous body said 'at the regular rate', which a payroll reader will implement as the base hourly rate — the very construction Loews argued for and lost. This understates what is owed.

assertions.text: meal periods must be recorded, the punches may not be rounded, and records showing a missed, short or delayed period raise a rebuttable presumption of a violation
assertions.note: Donohue v. AMN Services: 'We now consider whether time records showing noncompliant meal periods raise a rebuttable presumption of meal period violations at summary judgment. We hold they do.' Donohue also holds the presumption reaches short and delayed periods, not only missed ones, and that the employer may rebut it with evidence of bona fide relief or proper compensation.

assertions.text: §512 does not reach employees in certain occupations covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, or the motion picture and broadcasting agreements described in the section
assertions.note: §512(c)-(g) as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 95 (SB 693), effective January 1, 2026: construction occupations, commercial drivers, registered security officers, and employees of electrical, gas, water and local publicly owned electric utilities, each conditioned on a CBA meeting the terms in §512(e)(2); plus the wholesale baking and motion picture/broadcasting provisions in §512(c)-(d).

priorDefects: contradicted: 'A missed, late, or interrupted meal period entitles the employee to one additional hour of pay.' This is the ensure standard Brinker rejected. The premium is owed when the employer fails to PROVIDE a compliant period, not when a provided period is not taken.
understated: 'at the regular rate' — Ferra holds the measure is the regular rate of compensation, synonymous with the overtime regular rate, which takes in non-discretionary payments.
omitted: the waiver in §512(a) for both meal periods, and its conditions.
omitted: the on-duty meal period entirely (Wage Order 4 §11(A)).
omitted: the recording duty, the no-rounding rule and the rebuttable presumption (Donohue).
omitted: every collective-bargaining and industry carve-out in §512(c)-(g).
citation-gap: the clause cited 'IWC Wage Order (industry-specific)' — a body of law with no provision in it. Replaced with Order No. 4-2001 §11.
gaps: Order No. 4-2001 is the order read. The clause is inserted for every California employer, and the sixteen other IWC orders were not read. Where an employer is under Order 5 (public housekeeping), 7 (mercantile), 11 or 12 (motion picture/broadcasting) or 16 (construction/drilling/mining), the meal provision may differ and the rebuilt clause does not say so.

Whether a meal-period violation and a rest-period violation on the same workday are separately payable was not researched. §226.7(c) is drafted per period type, which suggests they are, but nothing read here decides it.

Whether a §512(a) waiver must be in writing was not resolved. Neither §512(a) nor Wage Order 4 §11(A) requires a writing for the waiver — only for an on-duty agreement — and the clause follows the text, but no source read here confirms that an oral waiver is safe.

Naranjo (2022) holds that premium pay is wages for §§201-203 and §226 purposes. The rebuilt emp_meal body does not carry that consequence; it is carried in emp_finalpay and hb_meal_rest instead. A reader of emp_meal alone will not learn that an unpaid premium becomes a waiting-time and wage-statement exposure.

judicialQuotations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. 2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004
judicialQuotations.quote: We conclude that under Wage Order No. 5 and Labor Code section 512, subdivision (a), an employer must relieve the employee of all duty for the designated period, but need not ensure that the employee does no work.

judicialQuotations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (Cal. 2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004
judicialQuotations.quote: the obligation to ensure employees do no work may in some instances be inconsistent with the fundamental employer obligations associated with a meal break: to relieve the employee of all duty and relinquish any employer control over the employee and how he or she spends the time.

judicialQuotations.case: Ferra v. Loews Hollywood Hotel, LLC (Cal. 2021) 11 Cal.5th 858
judicialQuotations.quote: We hold that the terms are synonymous: “regular rate of compensation” under section 226.7(c), like “regular rate of pay” under section 510(a), encompasses all nondiscretionary payments, not just hourly wages.

judicialQuotations.case: Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC (Cal. 2021) 11 Cal.5th 58
judicialQuotations.quote: We now consider whether time records showing noncompliant meal periods raise a rebuttable presumption of meal period violations at summary judgment. We hold they do.

judicialQuotations.case: Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC (Cal. 2021) 11 Cal.5th 58
judicialQuotations.quote: Moreover, AMN is incorrect that the presumption applies only to records showing missed meal periods; the presumption applies to records showing short and delayed meal periods as well. Providing employees with short or delayed meal periods is just as much a violation of the meal period provisions as failing to provide employees with a meal period at all.
